Header.CaseTitle: R (Harrison) v Secretary of State for Justice
Header.AppealFrom: High Court of Justice, King's Bench Division, Administrative Court

Party.n: The Secretary of State for Justice

SummaryOfPosition.Summary: The Appellant's challenge should be dismissed. The Court did not apply an incorrect legal test for violation of Article 2 Protocol 1 ECHR. The Court correctly found that the Appellant had not been denied effective access to educational facilities despite difficulties faced, and that the SSJ had committed significant resources to enabling distance learning participation including 25 hours a week in the Education Department with computer and internet access.

FactsReliedOn.item: The Appellant is serving a determinate sentence at HMP Wandsworth following conviction for robbery with a sentence of 8 years.
He commenced serving his sentence in 2019 and is eligible for release in 2027.
The Appellant enrolled in an Open University BA Social Sciences degree in September 2023.
He completed his second year of study prior to the April 2025 hearing despite the restrictions challenged.

The Appellant received significant support at HMP Wandsworth including a Distance Learning Coordinator, access to up to 25 hours per week in the Education Department library, and access to a shared laptop computer.
The Appellant benefited from the standard education budget allocation and had access to six books from the prison library at a time (the standard limit for distance learning students).

A meeting was held on 20 November 2024 between the Appellant's OU tutor, Student Support Officer, and prison education staff to discuss support arrangements and the implementation of the 50-page monthly limit.
The prison implemented the 50-page limit following a security incident on 15 September 2024 involving unauthorized materials being smuggled into the prison disguised as course materials.

Contentions.item: The Court did not apply an incorrect legal test for A2P1 violation. The correct test is whether the Appellant was denied effective access to such educational facilities as the state provides.
The Court recognised difficulties the Appellant faced but found that SSJ committed appropriate resources to enable participation in distance learning within security constraints.

The 50-page monthly limit was found unlawful as domestic administrative law but not as an A2P1 breach. The Court correctly found no A2P1 breach as the Appellant was not denied effective access to education.
The Court did not make an unlawful case management decision. The Judge excluded late evidence submitted just prior to hearing concerning alleged issues at a new prison facility.

The Open University course structure is specifically designed for distance learning and prisoners can complete courses with limited physical materials through online resources and provided course packs.

The prison dedicated resources to address operational issues as they arose, including enhanced library access hours, liaison with OU tutors, and facilitating alternative means of accessing course content.
The Judge's finding that strategies used were "sufficient to afford lawful access to education in the prison context" was correct and based on sound factual findings.

There was no evidence before the High Court that the 50-page limit or reduced library access meant the Appellant was denied effective access to his OU course, particularly given alternative means of accessing materials.
The Appellant successfully completed his second year examinations, achieving passing grades in all modules, which demonstrates effective access was maintained.

SourceExtracts.Quote: The Appellant is serving a determinate sentence following conviction for robbery. He enrolled in an Open University degree program designed specifically for distance learning in prison environments.
Prior to the April 2025 hearing, the Appellant completed his second year of study, successfully passing all module examinations despite the restrictions he challenges.
The Court found that the strategies employed were "sufficient to afford lawful access to education in the prison context" taking into account the security imperatives and resources available.

At HMP Wandsworth the Appellant had access to the Education Department library for up to 25 hours per week. While this represented a reduction from previous unlimited access, it remained substantially more than the minimum standard for distance learning prisoners.

The Open University course structure is specifically designed for prisoners. The materials are provided in modular course packs that minimize the need for extensive additional resources. Students can complete courses with the materials provided supplemented by limited library access.

The 50-page monthly limit was implemented following a specific security incident. While the Court found this restriction disproportionate under domestic administrative law, it did not amount to a denial of effective access to education under Article 2 Protocol 1.

The vast majority of prisoners undertaking higher education do so through Open University courses because these courses are designed for the prison environment. The Appellant's choice to study through the OU demonstrates engagement with the system designed to facilitate prisoner education.

There were operational accommodations made including: enhanced library sessions, liaison with OU tutors to prioritize essential materials within the 50-page limit, and access to digital materials through the Virtual Campus system where available.

OpposingArguments.item: The Appellant argues that any substantial interference with education access requires detailed justification. The Respondent contends that the correct test is whether there was denial of effective access, not whether every restriction was justified in minute detail.

The Appellant argues the Court should have considered all events post-dating the claim form as part of an ongoing violation. The Respondent submits this would impermissibly convert judicial review into ongoing monitoring and the Judge properly exercised case management discretion.

The Appellant contends that the 800-page course requirement cannot be satisfied with a 50-page monthly allowance. The Respondent notes that OU courses provide core materials in course packs and that additional reading, while beneficial, is not essential to complete the degree.

The Appellant argues library access of 1 hour fortnightly is manifestly inadequate. The Respondent submits that combined with 25 hours weekly education department access and other accommodations, overall provision remained adequate.

The Appellant relies on Mehmet Arslan regarding internet access. The Respondent distinguishes that case as involving complete denial of all computer/internet access making education impossible, whereas here the Appellant had substantial facility access.

SecurityConsiderations.item: The 50-page limit was implemented following a specific intelligence-led security incident on 15 September 2024 where contraband was concealed in bulk educational materials.
PSI 32/2012 requires balancing educational access against security imperatives including preventing smuggling of prohibited items and maintaining prison order.
The reduction in library hours was driven by staffing constraints following illness and unfilled vacancies in the education department, not a deliberate restriction on education.
Risk assessments conducted by the Security Department concluded that the 50-page limit, while restrictive, was proportionate to address the identified threat based on the September incident.
The Governor's evidence demonstrated that the restriction was kept under review and would be relaxed once the security situation permitted.

FactualDisputes.item: The Appellant claims he would have achieved higher grades without the restrictions. This is speculative and unsupported. He achieved passing grades in all modules.
The Appellant suggests the restrictions made completion of his course impossible. He in fact completed his second year successfully.
The Appellant characterizes library access as inadequate. The evidence shows he had 25 hours per week in the Education Department plus 1 hour fortnightly specifically for library materials.
The Appellant implies the restrictions were arbitrary. The evidence demonstrates they were implemented following a specific security incident and based on risk assessment.

ProportionalityAnalysis.item: The restrictions pursued the legitimate aim of maintaining prison security and preventing smuggling of contraband.
The means employed (50-page limit, reduced library hours) were rationally connected to that aim given the September 2024 security incident.
The restrictions went no further than necessary: the 50-page limit still allowed substantial material access, and accommodations were made to prioritize essential materials.
The balance struck was appropriate: the Appellant remained able to pursue his education (evidenced by successful completion of second year) while security concerns were addressed.
Less restrictive alternatives were considered but rejected on security grounds as insufficiently protective given the intelligence about smuggling methods.

ComparisonToOU.item: The Open University course structure is specifically designed for prison distance learning with minimal reliance on external resources.
OU course materials are provided in self-contained course packs that include all essential readings.
Additional reading beyond course packs is supplementary rather than essential for successful course completion.
The OU system demonstrates that effective higher education can be delivered in prison contexts with appropriate design.
The Appellant's ability to complete his OU course demonstrates the system works even with the security restrictions in place.
